title: Meeting Notes Email Integration: Granola vs Fathom vs Circleback
summary: Granola syncs meeting notes both ways but skips the transcript. Fathom, Circleback, Otter and Fireflies are read-only and carry the full record. Compared.
body_markdown:
Founders rarely lack information. They lack the time to move that information from a Zoom call into a follow-up email or a CRM record. Most meeting tools promise to solve this by recording everything. They drop a transcript into your inbox and call it progress. But a transcript is just more reading. If your meeting notes email integration requires you to open a separate dashboard or copy-paste text into a draft, the system is broken. You are still the manual labor in your own workflow.


Slashy documents meeting-notes integrations with five tools, and they split on one axis that matters more than any feature list. Granola syncs in both directions, so notes you write on an event in Slashy flow back to Granola, but it does not carry the transcript. Circleback, Fathom, Otter and Fireflies are read-only, and all four do carry the full transcript. That is the decision: a two-way notes workflow, or a verbatim record you can quote.


## Who Each Tool Is Actually Best For (Before You Read Any Further)


Granola suits you if you write notes during or after the call and want them to stay in one place. It is the only one of the five where the sync runs both ways: summary, notes and action items move in both directions, so an edit you make on the event in Slashy shows up in Granola the next time you open that meeting. Meeting title, time and attendees come across from Granola. The transcript does not.


Fathom suits you when the verbatim record is the point. Slashy pulls the meeting summary, the transcript and any action items Fathom captured, and attaches them to the matching calendar event under a Fathom section that expands to the full transcript. The connection is read-only, authorized over OAuth with read access to your meetings, so nothing you do in Slashy writes back to Fathom.


Circleback attaches three things to the matching event: the full transcript, the action items it extracted, and the participant list with any roles it identified. Action items become a checklist inside the event panel that you can tick off or hand to the agent to turn into reminders, follow-up emails or new events. Its documentation is explicit that Slashy reads from Circleback and never writes, so edits you make on an event in Slashy do not change anything on the Circleback side. Otter and Fireflies behave the same way, each syncing the full transcript, extracted action items and structured participant data including the role assigned to each speaker. If you are keeping deal records straight alongside this, the same event context is what feeds[logging deals from your inbox](https://www.slashy.com/blog/guides/attio-email-integration-log-deals-from-your-inbox-automatically) .


## How the Integration Works: Granola's Two-Way Sync vs One-Way Delivery


Direction of data flow is the difference that actually changes how you work, and it is easy to miss when every integration page uses the same word for both.


With the four read-only ones, the flow goes one way. Circleback, Fathom, Otter and Fireflies process the session and attach the results to the matching calendar event in Slashy. You read them there. But if you want to correct a summary or add a detail you remembered afterwards, you do it in that product, because nothing you write on the event travels back. Circleback's documentation puts it plainly: Slashy reads, and never writes.


Granola runs the return leg. Summary, notes and action items move in both directions, so a correction you make on the event in Slashy is in Granola the next time you open that meeting. The meeting note stays a live record rather than a receipt of what a tool thought it heard at the time.


This matters because the useful detail often lands after the call, not during it. A prospect names the budget in a reply, or the security review that has to happen first. On a two-way connection you write it once, onto the event, and both sides have it. On a one-way connection you write it twice or you lose it.


## What Gets Synced: A Criteria-by-Criteria Comparison


What you are really choosing is what lands on the event. A full transcript is a safety net to some people and noise to others, and the honest answer depends on whether you ever need to quote a call back. Here is what each connection actually carries, taken from what Slashy documents rather than from anyone's marketing page.


Criterion Granola Fathom Circleback Otter Fireflies


**Sync direction** Both ways Read-only Read-only Read-only Read-only


**Full transcript** No Yes Yes Yes Yes


**Summary and notes** Both ways Into Slashy Into Slashy Into Slashy Into Slashy


**Action items** Both ways Into Slashy Checklist on event Checklist on event Checklist on event


**Participant data** Attendees With the summary Names and roles Names and roles Names and roles


**Event matching** Calendar identifier Similar start window Similar times Similar times Similar times


**On disconnect** Notes stay on events Data removed Data removed Data removed Data removed


Two rows in that table do most of the work. If you need to check exactly what a client said in minute twenty-two, Granola will not have it and the other four will. If you want a note you write after the call to end up back in your notes app rather than stranded in your email client, Granola is the only one that does it.


The disconnect row is the one people find out about late. Turn Granola off and the notes already synced stay on your calendar events in Slashy and remain available to the agent. Turn off any of the other four and their data is removed from your events, though your data inside those products is untouched. If you are trialling tools, that difference decides what you still have afterwards.


## Transcripts, Summaries, and Action Items: What Lands in Your Email Client


Whichever you connect, the notes do not arrive as another email to process. They land in the event detail panel on the matching calendar event, next to the attendees, the location and the video link. That is the point of wiring them to the calendar rather than the inbox: the record sits on the meeting, not in a thread you have to find again.


All five connect the same way. Press Cmd and comma to open Settings, go to Integrations, then Meeting Notes, then the tool, and authorize it. Granola backfills your full history on the first sync rather than starting from that day, so give it a few minutes before you go looking for an older call.


Once notes are syncing, you can ask the agent about a past call in plain language. "What did we agree with Acme last week?" searches your connected meeting notes and comes back with an inline card showing the meeting, the date, the participants and a link to the recording. You are not opening another app to answer a question about your own meeting.


## Automation and Follow-Up: What Each Tool Can Trigger After a Meeting


A meeting note that just sits there is a wasted opportunity, and the action items are where that changes. With Circleback, Otter and Fireflies the extracted action items become a checklist on the event, and the ticked state persists. You can pull one into the agent to schedule it, send a follow-up email, or turn it into a reminder. With Granola the action items move in both directions, so ticking or adding one is a change Granola sees too.


From there the follow-up is a request rather than a writing job. Ask the agent to draft a reply to the meeting and it works from the action items already attached to that event, alongside your email and your existing memories, in the voice it has learned from your sent mail. Booking the next step runs the same way through the[AI meeting scheduler from email](https://www.slashy.com/blog/ai-meeting-scheduler-from-email-book-calls-without-the-back-and-forth) .


One limit applies to all of them. A recording with no calendar invite is kept but not attached to an event, and with Granola, notes on events you were not invited to do not sync at all. If a session was ad hoc, expect to associate it by hand from the dropdown on the event.


## The Honest Verdict: Two-Way Notes or a Verbatim Record


The honest version of this decision is short, because the documented differences are narrow. Pick Granola if you write notes yourself and want edits made on the event to travel back to your notes app, and if you can live without a transcript. Pick Fathom, Circleback, Otter or Fireflies if you need the verbatim record on the event and are content for the connection to run one way.


Among the four read-only ones, the differences that are actually documented are small: Circleback, Otter and Fireflies each bring structured participant data with speaker roles and turn action items into a checklist on the event, while Fathom brings the summary, transcript and action items together. Anything beyond that is a claim about those products rather than about how they connect here, and it is not ours to make.


One more thing worth weighing before you commit: Granola is the only one that leaves its notes behind on your events if you disconnect. The other four take their data off the events when you turn them off.


## Conclusion


The question is not which meeting tool records best. It is whether what it records ends up on the event you are looking at when you write the follow-up. Connect any of these five and it does, with the trade-off between a two-way notes loop and a verbatim transcript being the only real fork.


If you want to try it, Slashy starts with 7 days of full access. Connect the tool you already record with, and the notes are on the event before you open the draft.
